content: The FLORIDA trial aimed to evaluate the impact of fluvastatin on residual ischemia in patients who had experienced an acute myocardial infarction. This study was designed as a randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blinded, parallel trial. A total of 540 patients with acute myocardial infarction and serum cholesterol levels below 251 mg/dL were enrolled. Ambulatory electrocardiographic (AECG) monitoring was employed to assess ischemia over a 48-hour period at three time points: baseline, 6 weeks, and 12 months. Participants were randomly assigned to receive either fluvastatin or a placebo. After 12 months of treatment, the group receiving fluvastatin demonstrated a 13% reduction in total cholesterol (TC) levels and a 21% reduction in low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) levels. In contrast, the placebo group exhibited a 9% increase in total cholesterol levels. At baseline, AECG monitoring revealed ischemia in 11% of the patients. Among those with ischemia detected at baseline, 67% (32 out of 48 patients) no longer exhibited ischemia after 6 weeks of treatment, and 76% (35 out of 46 patients) showed no signs of ischemia after 12 months. Despite these findings, the study concluded that fluvastatin treatment did not significantly influence ischemia as detected by AECG or the occurrence of major clinical events when compared to placebo.
